8.title: your grandmother before dinner
8.hook: your grandmother before dinner; a gift you didn't earn
8.howItsDone: Many Catholic families say a short grace before meals, often the traditional "Bless us, O Lord," and many make the sign of the cross before and after it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sacramentals, faith you can hold. Week one is behind you. Week two starts with the thing all those small signs point to. Day eight.

The food is on the kitchen table, steam coming off the potatoes, and somebody's already reaching for the bread. Then a hand on the wrist. A grandmother, saying: wait. Grace first. Heads go down. A few quick words, a quick amen, and everybody eats. A kid at a table like that could grow up thinking grace means the little speech before dinner. It does. But the word is much bigger than the speech. It's the reason for the speech.
screen: `A KITCHEN TABLE.` → `WAIT. GRACE FIRST.` → `THE WORD IS BIGGER THAN THE SPEECH.`

segments.voice: Grace comes from the Latin gratia: a favor, a gift, something given freely, not paid for. It's the same root that gives English gratitude, and gratis, free of charge. The New Testament was written in Greek, and there the word is charis, which also means a gift freely given, and a kind of loveliness. So when Catholics talk about grace, they mean God's gift of himself, given before anybody earned it. The letter to the Ephesians says it plainly, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "For by grace you are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God." Not of yourselves. That's the surprise at the heart of the word. You don't climb up to grace. It comes down to you. Catholics say it arrives in many ways: in baptism and the other sacraments, in prayer, in an ordinary Tuesday when a friend calls at exactly the right moment. Yesterday's small signs are there to get a person ready for it. And here's where the dinner table comes back in. The traditional Catholic grace before meals goes: "Bless us, O Lord, and these thy gifts, which we are about to receive from thy bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen." Listen to what it notices. Thy gifts. Thy bounty. Somebody grew the food, somebody cooked it, and before any of that, Catholics say, somebody gave the world to begin with. So saying grace isn't paying a fee before eating. It's noticing that you were given something.
screen: `GRATIA — A FAVOR, A GIFT.` · `CHARIS — GIVEN FREELY.` · `NOT OF YOURSELVES.` · `THE TABLE IS A SMALL PICTURE.` · then, large: `A GIFT YOU DIDN'T EARN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, and it's small on purpose. Think of one thing you have today that you didn't earn. The air, maybe. A person. A roof. Let it come into focus, and stay with it while you breathe slowly. If you pray, you can say thank you with each breath out. If you don't, just let yourself notice the gift.
Grace. A favor, a gift freely given. Catholics say it comes first, before anyone earns it. Eighth word.
Your line: you are already held. Grace means the gift came first. That's day eight.

9.title: a young woman says yes
9.tomorrow: the words, line by line, from Luke
9.howItsDone: Catholics honor Mary as the Mother of God and ask for her prayers, especially in the Hail Mary and the rosary; the Annunciation, the angel's visit, has its own feast day each year.

segments.voice: Yesterday: grace, a gift you didn't earn. Your line was you are already held. Today the word comes back, in an angel's mouth. Day nine.

A small town in Galilee called Nazareth. A young woman there is promised in marriage to a man named Joseph. Luke doesn't give her age, and he doesn't describe the house. An ordinary day, as far as we know. And then, Luke's Gospel says, the angel Gabriel comes in to her, telling her she's going to have a child, and that he'll be called the Son of the Most High. She isn't married yet. Today, a yes the whole Catholic story leans on, and the young woman who said it.
screen: `A TOWN IN GALILEE.` → `AN ANGEL IN THE ROOM.` → `SHE ISN'T MARRIED YET.`

segments.voice: Her name, in Hebrew, was Miriam, like the sister of Moses. We say Mary. And the first thing Gabriel says to her, after the greeting, is what the angels in Luke say again and again: "Fear not, Mary, for thou hast found grace with God." Grace: yesterday's word, back again. Then she does something people skip over. She asks a question. How can this be? She isn't passive. She wants to understand. The angel answers, and then she gives the reply Catholics have treasured ever since. In the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." In Latin, be it done is fiat, and Catholics still call her answer Mary's fiat. Her yes. Here's why it matters so much. Catholics say God didn't force anything on her. He asked, and waited, and the whole story of Jesus turns on a young woman saying yes. That's why they call her the Mother of God, because they believe her son is God, and why she gets the highest honor of any saint: honor, as day five said, not worship. Other Christians differ on how much to say about her. Many Protestants honor her as a faithful believer and a model of trust, and don't pray to her. And Luke's page is the same for all of them: a young woman, a question, and then yes.
screen: `MIRIAM — FEAR NOT.` · `SHE ASKS A QUESTION.` · `FIAT — BE IT DONE.` · `THE MOTHER OF GOD.` · then, large: `BEHOLD THE HANDMAID OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Think of one thing in your life right now that you're resisting: something you can't change and keep pushing against. Name it. Notice how tightly you're holding it. Then, breath by breath, let your hands open a little on your lap. If you pray, you can borrow Mary's words: be it done to me.
Mary. Miriam of Nazareth, the mother of Jesus, whose yes, her fiat, Catholics honor above every other saint. Ninth word.
Your line: let it be. But notice the order: first she asked her honest question. Day nine.

10.title: the words, line by line, from Luke
10.hook: the words, line by line, from Luke
10.howItsDone: Catholics say the Hail Mary ten times on each decade of the rosary, and on its own at many moments of the day; its first half comes from Luke 1:28 and 1:42.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mary, a question, and then a yes. Your line was let it be. Today, the words on the rosary's ten beads, and who said them first. Day ten.

At a wake, a room full of voices runs it together until it sounds like one long word. A kid in Catholic school rattles it off before anyone can blink. In football, a desperate pass thrown deep with no time left still gets called a Hail Mary. Said that fast, it's easy to miss where the words came from. Half the prayer isn't new at all. It's lifted, line by line, from the first chapter of Luke's Gospel. Today, slowly.
screen: `ONE LONG WORD AT A WAKE.` → `A HAIL MARY PASS.` → `LIFTED FROM LUKE.`

segments.voice: The first line belongs to an angel: yesterday's Gabriel, in the room in Nazareth. In the Douay-Rheims Bible, his first words are: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." Hail is just an old hello. Full of grace is day eight's word, filled to the brim. The next line belongs to a relative. A little later in Luke, Mary visits her cousin Elizabeth, who's also pregnant, and Elizabeth cries out: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb." Over the centuries Christians put those two greetings side by side, an angel's and a cousin's, and added two names: Mary, right after the angel's hail, and Jesus at the end. That's the whole first half. Every word of it, apart from those two names, is from Luke. Then the prayer turns. The second half isn't scripture. It's the Church speaking, and it came into the prayer later: Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death. Amen. Listen to the shape. The first half says hello. The second half asks for something, small and huge at once: pray for us. Now, and at the very end. Catholics aren't asking Mary to do what only God does. They're asking her to pray with them. On the rosary it comes ten times in each decade, a greeting, then a request, like a heartbeat. Say it fast and it's a blur. Say it slowly and you're standing in two rooms in Luke's Gospel.
screen: `AN ANGEL'S HELLO.` · `A COUSIN'S BLESSING.` · `THEN THE CHURCH ASKS.` · `PRAY FOR US, NOW AND AT THE END.` · then, large: `A GREETING, THEN A REQUEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Let your breath slow down. On the breath in, think of a greeting: hello to someone you love. On the breath out, think of a request: one thing you need right now. In, a greeting. Out, a request. If you pray the Hail Mary, you can say it once, as slowly as you've ever said it.
The Hail Mary. An angel's hello and a cousin's blessing from Luke, then the Church's request: pray for us. Tenth word.
Your line: a greeting, then a request. Two rooms in Luke, ten times a decade. Day ten.

11.title: the family word he chose
11.tomorrow: why people stand up when the book comes in
11.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Our Father at every Mass, standing together before communion, at the start of each decade of the rosary, and in daily prayer, usually ending at "deliver us from evil."

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Hail Mary, a greeting, then a request. Today, the prayer on the single beads between the tens. Day eleven.

A boss gets the best email voice. A judge gets your honor. A king, in the old days, got your majesty, said from the knees. The more powerful someone is, the more careful and formal the words. In Luke's Gospel, a disciple asks Jesus: teach us to pray. How do you talk to the one who made the stars? Titles, you might expect. A long list of them. Instead he gives them a prayer that begins with a family word.
screen: `YOUR HONOR. YOUR MAJESTY.` → `TEACH US TO PRAY.` → `A FAMILY WORD.`

segments.voice: In Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims Bible, it starts: "Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name." Father. Behind the Greek of the Gospels, some scholars hear the Aramaic word abba. Mark's Gospel keeps that word untranslated, on the night before Jesus died, when he prays in the garden: "Abba, Father, all things are possible to thee." Abba is the word a son or daughter uses. Not a title. A relationship. And then look at the word before it: our. Not my Father. Our. Read it closely and there isn't a single I or me in the whole prayer. Give us. Forgive us. Lead us. Deliver us. Someone praying it alone at night still prays in the plural, standing in a crowd they can't see. That's the family word doing its work twice: God is not a stranger, and neither is the person next to you. At Mass, the whole room prays it together, just before communion. For a long time Catholics prayed it in Latin: Pater noster, our Father. One difference shows up in other churches. Churches that learned the prayer from the King James Bible end with: for thine is the kingdom, the power and the glory. The King James prints that line in Matthew; the Douay-Rheims, translated from the Latin, ends at deliver us from evil, and so do Catholics. At Mass, the priest adds a short prayer after it, and then everyone says a version of that ending together. Same prayer, two old habits.
screen: `ABBA — FATHER, AT HOME.` · `OUR, NOT MY.` · `NO I, NO ME.` · `PATER NOSTER.` · then, large: `NOT A STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Say just the first two words, slowly, out loud or silently: our Father. On our, think of someone you'd rather not include in that word, and include them anyway. On Father, notice how different it sounds from a title. If you pray the whole prayer, you can pray it once, very slowly.
The Our Father. The prayer Jesus taught, opening with a family word, with no I or me in it anywhere. Eleventh word.
Your line: not a stranger. Not God, and not the person beside you. See you tomorrow.

12.title: why people stand up when the book comes in
12.hook: why people stand up when the book comes in
12.howItsDone: At Mass, Catholics sit for the first readings and the psalm, then stand for the Gospel, often tracing small crosses on the forehead, lips and heart as it is announced.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Our Father, a prayer with no I or me in it. Your line was not a stranger. Today, back inside the Mass. Day twelve.

A guest at a Catholic Mass spends a lot of it half a second behind. Everyone else seems to know when to sit, when to stand, when to kneel, and the guest is watching the person in front. One moment in particular catches visitors off guard. People have been sitting quietly, listening to readings. Then music starts, often the word alleluia, and the whole room stands up at once. Someone at the front lifts a book up high. Why stand for a book? Day two was the table at the center of the Mass. Today, the first half: the story.
screen: `SIT, STAND, KNEEL.` → `THE WHOLE ROOM STANDS.` → `FIRST, THE STORY.`

segments.voice: First, the name. The word Mass is usually traced to the old Latin words at the end of the service, ite, missa est, roughly: go, you are sent. So the whole thing may be named for the moment people walk back out the door. Now, the first half. Catholics call it the Liturgy of the Word, and it's mostly listening. On a Sunday there's usually a reading from the Old Testament, then a psalm, often sung back and forth, then a reading from one of the letters of the apostles. People sit for those. Then comes the Gospel, a reading from one of the four books about the life of Jesus, and everyone stands. The English word Gospel goes back to an Old English phrase for good news, and it translates the Greek euangelion. Catholics say that when the Gospel is read, Christ himself is speaking to the people gathered there. So you stand the way you'd stand when someone important walks into the room. Right before it, people trace three little crosses with a thumb: on the forehead, on the lips, on the heart. It's day one's sign, shrunk down. One common way to explain it: may these words be in my mind, on my lips, in my heart. Standing for the reading isn't new, either. In the Bible itself, after the exile, the scribe Ezra opens the book of the law in front of the whole people, and when he opens it, they all stand up. Then everyone sits again, and a priest or deacon preaches: the homily. The story has entered the room.
screen: `MASS — GO, YOU ARE SENT.` · `READINGS, A PSALM, THEN THE GOSPEL.` · `THREE SMALL CROSSES.` · `EZRA OPENS THE BOOK. THEY STAND.` · then, large: `THE STORY ENTERS THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. If you're sitting, stand up, just for this, the way the room stands for the Gospel. Touch your forehead, your lips, your heart. Then sit back down, breathe slowly, and let each of those three places get ready to listen. You don't have to say anything.
The Gospel. The good news: the reading about the life of Jesus that everyone stands to hear, the high point of the Mass's first half. Twelfth word.
Your line: the story enters the room. That's why everyone gets to their feet. Day twelve.

13.title: "peace be with you"
13.hook: "peace be with you" — the handshake in the middle
13.tomorrow: the obligation nobody explains as a gift
13.howItsDone: At Mass, after the Our Father and before communion, the priest invites the people to offer each other a sign of peace, and people turn to those nearby with a handshake, a bow or a nod, saying "peace be with you."

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Gospel, and the whole room standing for the story. Today, the moment the whole room turns around. Day thirteen.

The Mass is quiet and formal. Candles, a priest at the altar, everyone facing forward, nobody talking. And then, out of nowhere, everyone turns around. The person behind you sticks out a hand. The teenager next to you, who hasn't looked up from the floor, says peace be with you. A couple kisses. A little kid waves at the whole row. For a few moments, a room full of people who mostly don't know each other shakes hands. Then everyone turns back to the front as if nothing happened. Today, the handshake in the middle of the Mass.
screen: `EVERYONE FACING FORWARD.` → `THEN EVERYONE TURNS AROUND.` → `THE HANDSHAKE IN THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: After the story comes the table. Bread and wine are carried up to the altar, the priest prays over them, and the whole room says the Our Father, from day eleven. Then, just before people come forward for communion, the sign of peace. Where does it come from? Start with Easter night. In John's Gospel, the frightened friends of Jesus are hiding behind locked doors, and the risen Jesus stands among them. His first words, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Peace be to you." Not a scolding for running away. Peace. In the Greek of John's Gospel it's eirene, a word that carries the old Hebrew greeting shalom, which means more than quiet. It means whole, complete, nothing missing. The first Christians greeted each other with more than a handshake: early Christian writers describe a kiss of peace shared in worship. There's a reason it sits right before communion in the Catholic Mass. Jesus once said that if you're bringing a gift to the altar and remember that someone has something against you, leave the gift there, go and make peace first, then come back. So before people go up to the table, they turn to whoever's beside them. Not their best friend. Whoever happens to be there. It's short on purpose. It isn't a chat. It's a sign: before we go any further, we're at peace with each other. The gesture varies from place to place: a bow, a nod, a handshake. The meaning holds.
screen: `AFTER THE STORY, THE TABLE.` · `PEACE BE TO YOU — EASTER NIGHT.` · `SHALOM — WHOLE, NOTHING MISSING.` · `MAKE PEACE, THEN COME TO THE ALTAR.` · then, large: `TURN TO THE STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Bring three people to mind, one at a time. Someone you love. Someone you barely know: a neighbor, a coworker, the person who sold you coffee. Then someone you're not at peace with right now. With each one, picture turning to them and offering your hand. If you pray, you can wish each of them peace.
The sign of peace. Turning to whoever is beside you, just before the table, to say peace be with you. Thirteenth word.
Your line: turn to the stranger. Not your best friend: whoever happens to be beside you. Day thirteen, done.

14.title: the obligation nobody explains as a gift
14.hook: the obligation nobody explains as a gift
14.carry: one day that isn't yours to fill
14.tomorrow: why there's fire in every church
14.howItsDone: Catholics are asked to attend Mass every Sunday (or on Saturday evening) and on certain holy days, and to keep the day for worship, family and rest as far as they can.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the sign of peace. Your line was turn to the stranger. And that's two weeks. This week: grace, Mary, the Hail Mary, the Our Father, the Gospel, the sign of peace. Day fourteen.

Being woken up too early. Scratchy church clothes. A parent at the bottom of the stairs saying: we're going, it's an obligation. That's how some people who grew up Catholic remember Sunday. Catholics are asked to go to Mass every Sunday, and to a kid it can sound like homework for the soul. Meanwhile the rest of the week is full. The phone that never stops. The laundry. The emails that arrive on Saturday night. What if the obligation was never meant as homework?
screen: `SCRATCHY CHURCH CLOTHES.` → `HOMEWORK FOR THE SOUL?` → `SUNDAY, EXPLAINED AS A GIFT.`

segments.voice: Start at the very beginning of the Bible. In Genesis, God makes the world in six days, and then, in the Douay-Rheims Bible, "he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done." God rests. Not, the tradition says, because he's tired. In the story, the day of rest is built into the world like a beam into a house. For the Jewish people it became the Sabbath, the seventh day, kept from sunset Friday to sunset Saturday, and Jewish families keep it still. Then something happened on a different day. All four Gospels put the empty tomb on the first day of the week, the day after the Sabbath. Christians began gathering on that first day to break bread, and came to call it the Lord's day. In Latin, dies Domini. In Spanish it's still domingo, in Italian domenica. An early Christian named Justin Martyr described it for outsiders: on the day called Sunday, everyone gathers, the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, bread and wine are brought and blessed, and there's a collection for widows and orphans. That's recognizably the Mass. So why call it an obligation? Catholics say it's the way the Church makes sure the gift actually gets opened. Left alone, a week fills every hour. The obligation holds one day open: for worship, for family, for rest, for a long meal. Sunday Mass can also be kept on Saturday evening, at what's called the vigil. And it isn't a trap: the Church itself says a serious reason, like being sick or caring for a baby, excuses you. The idea underneath is simple. One day a week isn't yours to fill.
screen: `HE RESTED ON THE SEVENTH DAY.` · `THE FIRST DAY: THE EMPTY TOMB.` · `DIES DOMINI — THE LORD'S DAY.` · `JUSTIN: ON THE DAY CALLED SUNDAY.` · then, large: `THE GIFT GETS OPENED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, and for this sit you have nothing to do. Nothing to fill. Put the phone face down, or out of reach. Let your hands rest open. Every time your mind reaches for a task, notice it, and set it down for later. If you pray, you can offer the time to God. If not, just let it be empty.
Sunday. The Lord's day, the day of the empty tomb, the day the Church keeps open for worship and rest. Fourteenth word.
Your line: one day that isn't yours to fill. That's what the obligation was protecting all along. Two weeks, done.

original.note: Greek: the Lord's day, from Revelation 1:10. Latin made it dies Domini.

trapdoor: what you thought: an obligation to sit through church.
what it means: one day held open, so the gift of rest and worship actually gets opened.
what a scholar hears: kyriake hemera in Revelation 1:10; Justin Martyr's First Apology 67 describing Sunday worship.
